domain: release engineering / GitOps supply-chain integrity (deployed-artifact-vs-published-source drift detection)
axioms: 'Published' is only as authoritative as the ref used to define it; a ref that can itself go stale (a failed fetch, a lagging mirror) inherits that staleness into every verdict built on it
There is always a lag between a commit landing and a deployment mechanism propagating it; a drift check that doesn't account for that lag will alarm on every ordinary release cycle
A comparison surface (roots, files, hashes) is a sampling decision; anything outside the sample is invisible drift, and anything noisy inside the sample degrades signal quality
Byte-identity to a reference is necessary but not sufficient for correctness -- an artifact can be byte-identical to a HEAD that is itself broken
A severity policy that downgrades repeated identical findings trades alert fatigue for the risk of a permanent failure going quiet exactly when it matters most
failure_mode: does not evaluate the session-identity register semantics of W1-W4, only the deployed-artifact drift-detection design of W5
not positioned to judge whether the structural grep test (W3) can be evaded by code-level syntax tricks
may apply general release-engineering caution around fetch failures that is more conservative than this specific internal tool's stakes warrant
